newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian aid conference hangs in balance.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian aid conference hangs in balance.

text.p: U.S. and international financial officials are struggling to persuade Bosnian Serb leaders to support economic laws needed to clear the way for a postwar fund-raising conference scheduled for next week, foreign experts said.
Serb leaders had yet to sign off on a package of economic legisation set down as a prerequisite for the donors' conference, despite threats that they may lose out on substantial reconstruction aid.
The much-delayed donors' conference, which is expected to raise some $1.4 billion for peacetime reconstruction in 1997, is scheduled for June 24-25 in Brussels.
A high-level World Bank delegation said it held talks over the past three days in a bid to persuade the Serbs to support a customs and tariffs law which they had initially endorsed.

"We very much hope that the donors' conference takes place as scheduled but we are not there yet and some urgent action is required on the custom tariffs point," Caio Koch-Weser, managing director of World Bank operations, told reporters.
"I urge all those who have to take these decisions to make these decision very speedily," he said.
Robert Gelbard, the U.S. envoy to former Yugoslavia, sent appeals to the Serbs to make good on earlier pledges or risk losing out on peacetime aid, diplomats said.
Bosnian Serb leaders put the donors' conference in jeopardy earlier this month when they reneged on agreements on the proposed economic laws.

Foreign experts said the Serbs refused to accept an interim solution on custom rates which was to be used for six months until a single rate could be agreed. They wanted the issue put on hold for six months instead.

Diplomats in Sarajevo believed that indicted war criminal and former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic, who retains significant behind-the-scenes influence in Serb territory, was behind the move.
One foreign expert, who asked not to be named, said Karadzic and his allies viewed the economic laws as an endorsement of Bosnian statehood which they fought to destroy for more than three years.
"They don't want to recognise the state authority because setting rates nationwide implies that you have external boundaries of Bosnia," said one expert.

With customs rates higher in the Serb entity than the Moslem-Croat federation, harmonising customs regulations would also cut into profits earned by state-run monopolies linked to Karadzic and his ruling party.
"It's about greed. They want those customs revenues for their businesses," said one Western official.

Diplomats said the crisis surrounding the economic laws provided a crucial test for major powers which issued tough warnings to Bosnia's former warring factions at a summit last month in Sintra, Portugal.
Conditioning financial aid on compliance with the Dayton peace treaty was touted at the summit as a way of exerting leverage over recalcitrant nationalist faction leaders.

If the Bosnian Serbs were willing to sacrifice hundreds of millions of dollars in aid for the sake of nationalist political goals, diplomats said the United States and European powers may have to reconsider their latest initiatives.
International officials are considering either holding the conference without the Serb leadership, postponing it once again, or cancelling it altogether, diplomats said.
